reference.one_line: 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis, two days after banding of bleeding oesophageal varices, now re-bleeding (haemoglobin 7.1, black stools) with worsening encephalopathy after ibuprofen and zolpidem.

handoff.summary: Dunstan Hesselgrave, 58, had six bands placed on bleeding oesophageal varices on 15 Nov and came to 3 West on 16 Nov. Since 06:10 today he has passed three black stools, the last two with maroon streaks; heart rate has gone from 86 to 110, blood pressure from 112/64 to 94/54, and haemoglobin from 8.3 at 05:10 to 7.1 at 11:40. He is drowsy, unsure of the date and has marked asterixis; he was alert and fully oriented at 20:00 last night, before zolpidem 5 mg at 22:40. He also received ibuprofen 600 mg at 21:10 and 03:50. The 12:50 progress note describes him as stable with brown stools, which does not match the record, so the team may not yet know he is re-bleeding.
to_do: Call the hepatology attending and the on-call endoscopist now: probable variceal re-bleed
Repeat blood count now and every 4 to 6 hours; confirm the type and screen (valid to 18 Nov) and that 2 units of red cells are available; transfuse 1 unit if haemoglobin is below 7.0 g/dL
Discontinue ibuprofen and zolpidem; keep acetaminophen at or below 2 g in 24 hours
Keep octreotide running at 50 micrograms/hour; do not stop it at 07:00 on 18 Nov as the note plans, and do not start carvedilol
Nothing by mouth for endoscopy; the 14:00 lactulose is due and he is slow to swallow, so ask the team about the route
Hourly vital signs, orientation and stool chart; consider a higher level of care
Update his wife Marit, who is due after 13:00
if_then: If he vomits blood, systolic pressure falls below 90 or heart rate rises above 120, then call the rapid response team and prepare for ICU transfer and airway protection
If haemoglobin is below 7.0 g/dL, then transfuse 1 unit of red cells and recheck; do not over-transfuse
If someone proposes plasma or platelets for the INR of 1.9 or platelets of 57, then decline unless hepatology asks: the standing order and consult say not to give them for the numbers alone
If tremor with sweating or agitation returns, then give lorazepam 1 mg as ordered and no other sedative
If he cannot be roused to voice, then check bedside glucose and call the physician at once

reference.brief_hospital_course: Mr Hesselgrave, 58, with alcohol-related cirrhosis (ascites since March 2026, no previous screening endoscopy, ibuprofen most days since August), presented on 15 Nov vomiting blood, with heart rate 124, blood pressure 84/50, haemoglobin 7.4 g/dL and lactate 4.6 mmol/L. He received two units of red cells, octreotide, ceftriaxone and pantoprazole, was intubated for airway protection, and had six bands placed on large oesophageal varices. He was extubated at 15:40 and haemoglobin rose to 8.9. Mild encephalopathy was treated with lactulose, and alcohol withdrawal with symptom-triggered lorazepam (two doses). He moved to 3 West on 16 Nov, where a diagnostic paracentesis showed no infection (neutrophils 62 cells/µL). Overnight on 16 to 17 Nov he was given ibuprofen 600 mg twice and zolpidem 5 mg once, both contrary to hepatology and addiction medicine advice. From 06:10 on 17 Nov he passed three black stools, the later ones with maroon streaks. Heart rate rose to 110, blood pressure fell to 94/54, urea nitrogen rose from 28 to 34 mg/dL and haemoglobin fell from 8.3 to 7.1 g/dL by 11:40, with new drowsiness and marked asterixis. This indicates early re-bleeding with worsening encephalopathy, although the 12:50 progress note records him as stable. At the time of writing octreotide continues, diuretics and carvedilol remain on hold, and urgent hepatology review and repeat endoscopy are required.

qa.q: How many bands were placed at endoscopy, and when?
qa.a: Six bands on large oesophageal varices on 15 Nov, procedure 10:40 to 11:05.

qa.q: At what haemoglobin should he be transfused, and with how much?
qa.a: 1 unit of red cells if haemoglobin is below 7.0 g/dL. The latest value is 7.1, so the order has not yet been triggered.

qa.q: What has his haemoglobin done since admission?
qa.a: 7.4 on arrival, 8.9 after two units, then 8.6, 8.3 at 05:10 on 17 Nov and 7.1 at 11:40: a fall of 1.2 g/dL in six and a half hours.
evidence: labs: blood count, all five time points

qa.q: How have heart rate and blood pressure changed over the last three sets of vital signs?
qa.a: 04:00: 86 and 112/64. 08:00: 98 and 104/60. 12:00: 110 and 94/54. Heart rate rising and pressure falling.

qa.q: What stools have been charted since he reached the ward?
qa.a: Dark brown at 16:00 and brown at 20:00 on 16 Nov (19:40 in the nursing note), then black and loose at 06:10 on 17 Nov, and black, tarry with maroon streaks at 09:30 and 11:50.
evidence: flowsheet: liver and bleeding monitoring, stool colour row

qa.q: When was zolpidem given, and what was his mental state before and after?
qa.a: Zolpidem 5 mg at 22:40 on 16 Nov. He was alert and fully oriented at 20:00, hard to rouse at 04:00, and drowsy and unsure of the date with marked asterixis at 08:00 and 12:00.
evidence: flowsheet: mental state and asterixis rows

qa.q: How long is it since his last drink, and is he still in the withdrawal risk window?
qa.a: Last drink was the evening of 14 Nov; the addiction consult counted about 43 hours at 16:10 on 16 Nov, so about 65 hours now. Risk runs to about 72 to 96 hours, so yes.

qa.q: Which pain medicines has he received in the last 24 hours?
qa.a: Acetaminophen 500 mg at 16:30 on 16 Nov, and ibuprofen 600 mg at 21:10 on 16 Nov and 03:50 on 17 Nov.
evidence: meds: acetaminophen and ibuprofen as-needed records

qa.q: Did the paracentesis show spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
qa.a: No. Neutrophils were 62 cells/µL (threshold 250), Gram stain showed no organisms and culture has no growth at 24 hours. The sample was taken after two doses of ceftriaxone.

qa.q: The progress note attributes today's drowsiness to too little lactulose. Does the chart support that?
qa.a: Not well. He had been passing stools on lactulose three times daily and was fully oriented at 20:00. The change followed zolpidem at 22:40 and coincides with new black stools, a rising urea nitrogen (28 to 34) and a falling haemoglobin, which point to a sedative plus fresh blood in the gut.
evidence: flowsheet: stool and mental state rows
labs: chemistry and blood count 17 Nov

qa.q: Should the INR of 1.9 be corrected with plasma now that he may be bleeding again?
qa.a: Not for the number alone. The hepatology consult explains that INR does not measure bleeding risk in cirrhosis and plasma raises portal pressure; platelets 57 and fibrinogen 172 are above the stated replacement levels of 50 and 120. Any change is a hepatology decision.
evidence: labs: liver panel and blood count 17 Nov

qa.q: Is it safe to follow the plan to stop octreotide at 07:00 tomorrow and start carvedilol?
qa.a: No. That plan assumed no re-bleeding. With black stools, haemoglobin 7.1, heart rate 110 and blood pressure 94/54, octreotide should continue and a beta-blocker should wait until bleeding is controlled.

qa.q: Was a physician told about the black stool at 06:10?
qa.a: The chart does not record it. The night nurse wrote that it would be passed on at handover; there is no note of a physician being called then or after the 09:30 and 11:50 stools, despite the standing order.

qa.q: Who requested the 11:40 blood count, and why?
qa.a: The chart does not say. The routine order is daily at 05:00; no order or note explains the late-morning sample.

qa.q: What was his blood alcohol level on arrival?
qa.a: Not recorded. No ethanol level appears in the results; the history gives only the last drink as the evening of 14 Nov.

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: The re-bleed was recognised only when his wife arrived and could not wake him. The resident found the haemoglobin of 7.1, stopped ibuprofen and zolpidem and called the attending, but at 15:40 he vomited a large amount of fresh blood and his blood pressure fell to 76/44. He was intubated in the ICU. Endoscopy showed bleeding from an ulcer where a band had come away; further bands and a balloon tube failed to hold it, and an emergency shunt through the liver was placed that night after six more units of red cells. The bleeding stopped, but aspiration pneumonia, kidney failure and progressive liver failure followed, and he never regained consciousness. He was not a transplant candidate. After a family meeting care was directed at comfort, and he died on 26 Nov with his wife beside him. The team disclosed the medication and escalation failures to her, and a safety review was opened.

events.event: Wife arrives and cannot wake him; nurse calls the resident. Heart rate 118, blood pressure 88/50.
Resident at bedside reviews the 11:40 haemoglobin of 7.1; ibuprofen and zolpidem discontinued; attending and endoscopist called.
Vomits about 400 mL of fresh blood; blood pressure 76/44; rapid response call. Haemoglobin 6.2.
Transferred to Medical ICU and intubated; transfusion started.
Emergency endoscopy: bleeding post-banding ulcer; three more bands, bleeding slowed but not stopped; balloon tamponade tube placed.
Emergency shunt through the liver placed by interventional radiology; bleeding controlled. Six units of red cells since the afternoon.
Attending meets his wife and discloses that ibuprofen and a sleeping tablet were given against advice and that the black stool was not escalated.
Temperature 38.6 °C, right lower lobe aspiration pneumonia; antibiotics broadened.
Creatinine 2.4 mg/dL with falling urine output; albumin and vasoconstrictor treatment started.
Bilirubin 19 mg/dL, INR 3.1, creatinine 3.8 mg/dL, Glasgow Coma Scale 6 off sedation. Transplant team: not a candidate.
Family meeting with wife and brother; code status changed to comfort-focused care.
Died in the Medical ICU, wife present.

outcomes_30_day.notable: Died in hospital on day 11 of liver and kidney failure after an early variceal re-bleed recognised about nine hours late.

portal_messages.subject: Missed liver appointment and camera test
portal_messages.body: This is Marit, Dunstan's wife, writing on his account. I'm sorry he missed the clinic and the camera test yesterday. He is drinking again and wasn't fit to come. Can they be booked again? Also his back has been bad since he fell in August and he takes ibuprofen from the pharmacy most days, sometimes three times. Is that all right with his liver? He isn't taking the water tablets every day either. I don't know what else to do.
ideal_reply_points: Rebook the liver clinic and the screening endoscopy and confirm how the dates will reach them
Ask him to stop ibuprofen: bleeding and kidney risk in cirrhosis; acetaminophen up to 2 g a day is the safer choice
Encourage taking the diuretics daily and offer the alcohol service again
Give red flags: vomiting blood, black stools, confusion, swollen belly with fever mean emergency care
Acknowledge how hard this is for her

portal_messages.subject: Re: Missed liver appointment and camera test
portal_messages.body: Dear Mrs Hesselgrave, thank you for letting us know, and please don't apologise. New dates for the clinic and the endoscopy are in the post. Please ask Dunstan to stop the ibuprofen: with his liver it can cause bleeding and harm the kidneys. Acetaminophen is safer, no more than 2 g (four 500 mg tablets) in a day. The water tablets work best taken every morning. If he vomits blood, passes black sticky stools or becomes confused, call an ambulance; do not wait for us. Our alcohol nurse can ring you both if he agrees.
ideal_reply_points: Confirms rebooking
Clear instruction to stop ibuprofen with a safe alternative and dose limit
Emergency warning signs stated plainly
Offers alcohol support without judgement

portal_messages.subject: Black stools - should we wait for Monday?
portal_messages.body: Marit again. Since yesterday Dunstan's stools have been black and sticky like tar and they smell terrible. He went dizzy getting up from the sofa this morning and had to sit down. He's still drinking and still taking the ibuprofen for his back, I couldn't get him to stop. He says it's the beer and won't let me call anyone. I know the clinic is shut at the weekend. Is it all right to wait and ring on Monday, or is this one of the things you warned me about?
ideal_reply_points: This cannot wait: black tarry stools with dizziness in a man with cirrhosis means bleeding until proved otherwise
Call an ambulance or go to the emergency department now
No more ibuprofen or alcohol; nothing to eat on the way
A portal inbox is not monitored at weekends: the system should direct such messages to an urgent line
Yes, this is exactly the warning sign she was told about

portal_messages.subject: What happened to my husband on Tuesday?
portal_messages.body: On Monday Dunstan was sitting up talking to me and the alcohol doctor. On Tuesday afternoon I couldn't wake him and then he was sick with blood everywhere. Now he's on a breathing machine and they've put a tube through his liver. One of the nurses said he'd been given a sleeping tablet and ibuprofen in the night. The alcohol doctor told us on Monday, in front of me, no sleeping tablets. I need someone to explain how this happened and whether he is going to wake up.
ideal_reply_points: Respond the same day and offer a face-to-face meeting with the attending
Be honest: both medicines were given against the specialists' advice and the black stool was not escalated; a review is under way
Explain the shunt in plain words: a channel through the liver to take pressure off the bleeding veins
Do not predict the outcome by message; say who will update her daily
Offer support: social work, chaplaincy, patient relations

portal_messages.subject: Re: What happened to my husband on Tuesday?
portal_messages.body: Dear Mrs Hesselgrave, you deserve a full answer in person and I will be in the ICU family room at 16:00 today; if another time is better, tell the ICU nurse. You are right. He was given a sleeping tablet and ibuprofen overnight when our own advice said he should have neither, and the black stool on Tuesday morning should have been acted on sooner. I am sorry. We are reviewing exactly how this happened and I will share what we find. The tube is a shunt that lowers the pressure in the veins that bled. He remains very seriously ill.
ideal_reply_points: Apology and plain acknowledgement of the errors
Named person, time and place for a meeting
Short lay explanation of the shunt
Honest that he is critically ill without false reassurance

portal_messages.subject: Records and the review
portal_messages.body: I don't know if anyone still reads this now that Dunstan has died. Dr Ferreira-Nkemelu said there would be a review of what happened that night and that I would be told the findings. I would like a copy of his records from this admission and to know when the review will finish. His brother wants to come to the meeting too. I'm not sleeping much. I keep thinking I should have rung the ambulance on the Saturday instead of writing a message.
ideal_reply_points: Condolences, and confirmation that the message has been read by a named person
How to request the records and who in patient relations will handle it
Expected date of the review findings and an invitation for her and his brother
Reassure her that she did not cause this; she sought help
Offer bereavement support and ask gently how she is coping; suggest her own doctor if sleep does not improve

conversation.setting: Bedside on 3 West, afternoon of 16 Nov, about an hour after the 14:20 lorazepam dose; addiction medicine consultation

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Mr Hesselgrave? I'm Dr Nwosu-Hartmann, from the addiction medicine team. The liver doctors asked me to come by. Is now all right?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yeah. Go on. Bit slow today, sorry.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: No rush at all. And you are?

turns.speaker: Wife
turns.text: Marit. I'm his wife.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Good to meet you. Dunstan, are you happy for Marit to stay while we talk about the drinking?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: She knows all of it anyway.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Okay. First, just so I know how your head is today, where are we, and what's the date?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Hospital. Up on the ward now, not the intensive care. It's... Monday. The sixteenth.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Spot on. So tell me about the drinking in your own words. When did it start?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: My twenties, really. Just beers then. It got, it got heavier after the warehouse let me go.

turns.speaker: Wife
turns.text: That was 2024.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: And these days, a typical day?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Half a bottle of vodka. The small one, the three seven five. And some beers.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: How many beers?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Three. Four, maybe.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: So about twelve drinks a day all told. When was the very last one?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Saturday evening. Before all the, before the blood.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Saturday the fourteenth, in the evening. So that's about forty-three hours ago. At home, first thing in the morning, how are your hands?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Shaky. Till I've had one.

turns.speaker: Wife
turns.text: That's been going on a year at least, the shakes.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Have you ever had a fit when you stopped? Or seen or heard things that weren't there?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Never.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Have you stopped properly before?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Did a detox. A supervised one, 2024. Four months dry after that.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Four months is real, you've done it once. Anything else? Other drugs, cigarettes?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No drugs. Ten a day, the cigarettes.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Would a nicotine patch help while you're stuck in here?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Not now. Maybe later.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: That's fine, the offer stands. How has your mood been?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Low. Pretty low.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Low enough that you've thought about harming yourself?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No. Nothing like that.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Thank you for being straight with me. Right now I can see a fine shake in your hands, you're a bit sweaty and a bit on edge. The nurse gave you a lorazepam at twenty past two. That's the second one, there was one in the small hours as well.

turns.speaker: Wife
turns.text: Can't he just have something regular, to keep him settled? And to sleep? He hardly slept last night.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: I understand why you'd ask. Here's the problem. His liver is already making him a little foggy, and any sedative can tip that over and hide the withdrawal from us. So he gets lorazepam only when we can see it, shaking with sweating, or agitation. No regular doses, and no sleeping tablets at all. For sleep it's lights down, ear plugs, a quiet room.

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: No sleeping tablets.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: None. Can you tell me back why?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Because the liver makes me muddled. And tablets make it worse.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Exactly that. The risky stretch runs to three or four days after the last drink, so we keep watching. You're getting a vitamin every day too, thiamine. Now, after here. Would you come to our outpatient programme, and see the alcohol nurse at the liver clinic?

turns.speaker: Patient
turns.text: Yeah. I'll go. I have to, don't I.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: I think you do, and I think you can. There's also a tablet, acamprosate, that takes the edge off the craving. We can start it before you leave if your kidneys stay fine.

turns.speaker: Wife
turns.text: I'll make sure he gets there.

turns.speaker: Dr. Nwosu-Hartmann
turns.text: Good. I'll be back to see you both on Wednesday.
